Insight: Younger applicants showed substantially higher observed repayment difficulty; the age relationship decreased almost monotonically.
The highest income quintile had the lowest observed difficulty rate, while the relationship was not perfectly linear.
Medium credit groups were riskier than both extremes; credit amount alone was not enough to explain risk.
Credit-to-income quintiles showed a non-linear relationship with TARGET.
Applicants without bureau history had a higher observed repayment-difficulty rate than applicants with bureau history.
Applicants with at least one overdue bureau credit had roughly twice the observed repayment-difficulty rate.
Any overdue history was informative, but longer overdue duration did not create a monotonic increase in current TARGET rate.
Observed difficulty generally increased as bureau debt became larger relative to applicant income.
Previously refused applications were associated with a higher current repayment-difficulty rate than approved applications.
Late-payment rate alone was weak and non-monotonic in univariate EDA.
Average payment delay was weak/non-monotonic on its own.
A feature can be weak in univariate EDA yet still receive model importance because tree models capture interactions.
InterpretationNote: EDA importance and model importance are not identical
